items.truth: Speed is distance travelled per unit time.
items.lie: Speed is displacement per unit time.
items.explanation: Speed uses distance; average velocity uses displacement.

items.truth: Velocity includes direction.
items.lie: Velocity describes magnitude only.
items.explanation: Velocity is a vector: both magnitude and direction matter.

items.truth: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
items.lie: Acceleration is the rate of change of position.
items.explanation: Changing position gives velocity; changing velocity gives acceleration.

items.truth: The SI unit of speed is metres per second.
items.lie: The SI unit of speed is metres per second squared.
items.explanation: m/s measures speed; m/s² measures acceleration.

items.truth: Negative velocity can describe motion to the left when right is positive.
items.lie: Negative velocity always means an object is slowing down.
items.explanation: The sign identifies direction relative to the chosen positive direction.

items.truth: A car travelling 100 m in 20 s has an average speed of 5 m/s.
items.lie: A car travelling 100 m in 20 s has an average speed of 20 m/s.
items.explanation: Average speed = 100 ÷ 20 = 5 m/s.

items.truth: Travelling 3 m east then 3 m west gives a total distance of 6 m.
items.lie: Travelling 3 m east then 3 m west gives a total distance of 0 m.
items.explanation: Distance adds the lengths of both parts of the journey.

items.truth: Travelling 3 m east then 3 m west gives zero displacement.
items.lie: Travelling 3 m east then 3 m west gives a displacement of 6 m east.
items.explanation: Displacement depends only on final position minus initial position.

items.truth: A speedometer indicates instantaneous speed.
items.lie: A speedometer indicates the total distance travelled.
items.explanation: Instantaneous speed describes how fast the vehicle is moving at that moment.

items.truth: The gradient of a position–time graph gives velocity.
items.lie: The gradient of a position–time graph gives acceleration directly.
items.explanation: Velocity is change in position divided by elapsed time.

items.truth: A steeper positive position–time gradient means a greater positive velocity.
items.lie: A steeper positive position–time gradient means a smaller positive velocity.
items.explanation: A larger rise in position per second means greater velocity.

items.truth: The gradient of a velocity–time graph gives acceleration.
items.lie: The gradient of a velocity–time graph gives distance.
items.explanation: Acceleration is change in velocity divided by elapsed time.

items.truth: Signed area under a velocity–time graph gives displacement.
items.lie: Signed area under a velocity–time graph gives acceleration.
items.explanation: Velocity multiplied by time has units of displacement; negative areas subtract.

items.truth: Area under a speed–time graph gives distance travelled.
items.lie: Area under a speed–time graph gives average acceleration.
items.explanation: Adding speed multiplied by small time intervals gives total distance.

items.truth: A horizontal velocity–time line above zero means constant positive velocity.
items.lie: A horizontal velocity–time line above zero means the object is at rest.
items.explanation: Velocity is constant but non-zero; acceleration is zero.

items.truth: An object moving in the positive direction slows down if its acceleration is negative.
items.lie: An object moving in the positive direction speeds up if its acceleration is negative.
items.explanation: Acceleration opposite to velocity reduces speed while the object continues in that direction.

items.truth: An object moving in the negative direction speeds up if its acceleration is also negative.
items.lie: An object moving in the negative direction must slow down when acceleration is negative.
items.explanation: Acceleration in the same direction as velocity increases its magnitude.

items.truth: A ball thrown vertically upwards has downward acceleration at its highest point, ignoring air resistance.
items.lie: A ball thrown vertically upwards has zero acceleration at its highest point.
items.explanation: Its velocity is momentarily zero, but gravity still acts downwards.

items.truth: At constant speed, doubling the travel time doubles the distance travelled.
items.lie: At constant speed, doubling the travel time halves the distance travelled.
items.explanation: Distance = speed × time.

items.truth: At constant speed, doubling the distance doubles the travel time.
items.lie: At constant speed, doubling the distance halves the travel time.
items.explanation: Time = distance ÷ speed.

items.truth: An average speed of 10 m/s does not require a speed of 10 m/s throughout the trip.
items.lie: An average speed of 10 m/s means the speed was exactly 10 m/s throughout the trip.
items.explanation: Different instantaneous speeds can produce the same total-distance-to-time ratio.

items.truth: A passenger can be at rest relative to a train while moving relative to the ground.
items.lie: An object at rest relative to a train must also be at rest relative to the ground.
items.explanation: Motion depends on the reference frame.

items.truth: For a straight-line journey without reversing, distance equals the magnitude of displacement.
items.lie: For a straight-line journey without reversing, distance is always greater than the magnitude of displacement.
items.explanation: With no reversal, the path length equals the separation of the endpoints.

items.truth: A displacement can be negative in a chosen coordinate system.
items.lie: Distance travelled can be negative if an object moves backwards.
items.explanation: Displacement is signed; distance is a non-negative path length.

items.truth: A change from 2 m/s to 8 m/s in 3 s gives an average acceleration of 2 m/s².
items.lie: A change from 2 m/s to 8 m/s in 3 s gives an average acceleration of 6 m/s².
items.explanation: Average acceleration = (8 − 2) ÷ 3 = 2 m/s².

items.truth: In ideal projectile motion, horizontal velocity remains constant when air resistance is ignored.
items.lie: In ideal projectile motion, gravity steadily reduces horizontal velocity.
items.explanation: Gravity acts vertically; there is no horizontal acceleration in this model.

items.truth: A runner completing one lap has zero average velocity over that lap.
items.lie: A runner completing one lap must have zero average speed over that lap.
items.explanation: The displacement is zero, but the distance travelled is positive.

items.truth: An object can have zero displacement after travelling a non-zero distance.
items.lie: An object with zero displacement must have travelled zero distance.
items.explanation: A return journey ends at its starting point. Displacement is zero, but the distance travelled is not.

items.truth: An object can accelerate while its speed stays constant.
items.lie: An object cannot accelerate unless its speed changes.
items.explanation: Acceleration is a change in velocity. Changing direction at constant speed, as in uniform circular motion, is acceleration.

items.truth: A horizontal line on a position–time graph represents an object at rest.
items.lie: A horizontal line on a position–time graph represents constant non-zero speed.
items.explanation: The gradient of a position–time graph is velocity. A horizontal line has zero gradient.

items.truth: A force is a vector quantity.
items.lie: A force has magnitude but no direction.
items.explanation: Forces have both size and direction; direction matters when finding the resultant.

items.truth: Force is measured in newtons.
items.lie: Force is measured in kilograms.
items.explanation: The newton is the SI force unit; the kilogram measures mass.

items.truth: Two equal forces in opposite directions on the same object can balance.
items.lie: Two equal forces in the same direction on the same object cancel out.
items.explanation: Opposite forces subtract; forces in the same direction add.

items.truth: A non-zero net force causes acceleration.
items.lie: A non-zero net force is required to maintain constant velocity.
items.explanation: Newton’s second law links net force to acceleration, not velocity.

items.truth: For a fixed mass, doubling the net force doubles the acceleration.
items.lie: For a fixed mass, doubling the net force halves the acceleration.
items.explanation: From F = ma, acceleration is proportional to net force for a fixed mass.

items.truth: For a fixed net force, doubling the mass halves the acceleration.
items.lie: For a fixed net force, doubling the mass doubles the acceleration.
items.explanation: From a = F/m, greater mass produces less acceleration for the same net force.

items.truth: A 2 kg object with a net force of 6 N has an acceleration of 3 m/s².
items.lie: A 2 kg object with a net force of 6 N has an acceleration of 12 m/s².

items.truth: Inertia is an object’s resistance to changes in velocity.
items.lie: Inertia is a force that pushes moving objects forwards.
items.explanation: Inertia is a property associated with mass, not an additional force.

items.truth: An object with greater mass has greater inertia.
items.lie: An object with greater speed necessarily has greater inertia.
items.explanation: In introductory mechanics, inertia depends on mass, not speed.

items.truth: Newton’s third-law force pairs act on different objects.
items.lie: Newton’s third-law force pairs cancel because they act on the same object.
items.explanation: Each force acts on one of the two interacting objects.

items.truth: When a person pushes a wall, the wall pushes back on the person.
items.lie: When a person pushes a stationary wall, the wall exerts no force on the person.
items.explanation: The interaction produces equal-magnitude, opposite-direction forces on different objects.

items.truth: Earth pulls an apple downwards and the apple pulls Earth upwards.
items.lie: Earth pulls an apple downwards but the apple exerts no gravitational force on Earth.
items.explanation: Gravity is mutual. Earth’s much larger mass makes its acceleration tiny.

items.truth: The normal force acts perpendicular to a contact surface.
items.lie: The normal force always acts vertically upwards.
items.explanation: Normal means perpendicular to the surface, including tilted surfaces.

items.truth: Friction can prevent surfaces from sliding relative to each other.
items.lie: Friction exists only after surfaces start sliding.
items.explanation: Static friction can act before sliding begins.

items.truth: Static friction can be smaller than its maximum possible value.
items.lie: Static friction always equals its maximum possible value.
items.explanation: Static friction adjusts to balance the required tangential force up to its limiting value.

items.truth: Sliding friction usually converts some mechanical energy into internal energy.
items.lie: Sliding friction destroys energy completely.
items.explanation: Energy is transferred into microscopic motion and other forms; total energy is conserved.

items.truth: Air resistance acts opposite to an object’s velocity relative to the air.
items.lie: Air resistance always acts vertically upwards.
items.explanation: Its direction depends on the object’s motion relative to the air.

items.truth: At terminal velocity, a falling object has zero net force.
items.lie: At terminal velocity, gravity stops acting on a falling object.
items.explanation: Weight is balanced by opposing forces, so acceleration is zero.

items.truth: A parachute can reduce terminal speed by increasing drag.
items.lie: A parachute reduces terminal speed by eliminating gravity.
items.explanation: The parachute increases air resistance; weight remains.

items.truth: Pressure is force divided by area.
items.lie: Pressure is force multiplied by area.
items.explanation: P = F/A, so pressure depends on how concentrated the force is.

items.truth: For the same force, a smaller contact area gives greater pressure.
items.lie: For the same force, a smaller contact area gives smaller pressure.
items.explanation: Dividing the same force by a smaller area gives a larger pressure.

items.truth: A lever can reduce the effort force needed by increasing the effort distance.
items.lie: A lever reduces the required force without changing distance or energy transfer in an ideal machine.
items.explanation: Mechanical advantage trades force against distance; it does not create energy.

items.truth: A stretched string can exert tension on an attached object.
items.lie: A slack string can push an attached object away by tension.
items.explanation: Tension pulls along a taut string; a string does not transmit a compressive push in this way.

items.truth: Magnetic forces can act without direct contact.
items.lie: Magnetic forces require the magnet to touch the affected object.
items.explanation: A magnetic field allows interactions across a separation.

items.truth: Like magnetic poles repel.
items.lie: Like magnetic poles attract.
items.explanation: North repels north and south repels south; unlike poles attract.

items.truth: A floating object at rest has an upward buoyant force equal to its weight.
items.lie: A floating object at rest has an upward buoyant force greater than its weight.
items.explanation: Balanced vertical forces give zero vertical acceleration.

items.truth: For a frictionless ramp, increasing the angle increases the downhill acceleration between 0° and 90°.
items.lie: For a frictionless ramp, increasing the angle decreases the downhill acceleration.
items.explanation: The downhill component of gravity gives a = g sin θ.

items.truth: Balanced forces can act on an object moving at constant velocity.
items.lie: An object moving at constant velocity must have an unbalanced force acting on it.
items.explanation: Zero net force means zero acceleration. The object can remain at rest or move at constant velocity.

items.truth: Mass and weight are different physical quantities.
items.lie: Mass and weight are the same physical quantity.
items.explanation: Mass is measured in kilograms. Weight is a gravitational force measured in newtons and depends on gravitational field strength.

items.truth: In a vacuum, objects released from rest at the same place fall with the same acceleration regardless of mass.
items.lie: In a vacuum, heavier objects released from rest fall with greater acceleration than lighter objects.
items.explanation: At the same location, gravitational acceleration is independent of the falling object’s mass when other forces are absent.

items.truth: Kinetic energy is energy associated with motion.
items.lie: Kinetic energy is energy associated only with height.
items.explanation: Motion contributes kinetic energy; height in a gravitational field contributes gravitational potential energy.

items.truth: At the same speed, doubling mass doubles kinetic energy.
items.lie: At the same speed, doubling mass halves kinetic energy.
items.explanation: Kinetic energy = ½mv², so it is proportional to mass at fixed speed.

items.truth: For a fixed mass, doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy.
items.lie: For a fixed mass, doubling speed only doubles kinetic energy.
items.explanation: Speed is squared in ½mv².

items.truth: A book raised higher near Earth’s surface gains gravitational potential energy.
items.lie: Raising a book higher near Earth’s surface reduces its gravitational potential energy.
items.explanation: Near the surface, the increase is mgh for a height increase h.

items.truth: The joule is a unit of energy.
items.lie: The watt is a unit of energy.
items.explanation: Joules measure energy; watts measure energy transferred per second.

items.truth: Power is the rate of energy transfer.
items.lie: Power is the total energy stored in an object.
items.explanation: Power describes how quickly energy is transferred, not how much is stored.

items.truth: A device transferring 100 J in 5 s has a power of 20 W.
items.lie: A device transferring 100 J in 5 s has a power of 500 W.
items.explanation: Power = energy ÷ time = 100 ÷ 5.

items.truth: One watt is one joule per second.
items.lie: One watt is one joule multiplied by one second.
items.explanation: A watt measures a rate of energy transfer.

items.truth: An object can store energy without moving.
items.lie: An object must be moving to have any energy.
items.explanation: Gravitational, elastic and chemical stores can exist in stationary objects.

items.truth: Chemical reactions can transfer energy to the surroundings.
items.lie: Every chemical reaction must absorb energy from the surroundings.
items.explanation: Exothermic reactions transfer energy out; endothermic reactions absorb it.

items.truth: Food provides a chemical energy store.
items.lie: Food stores energy as a supply of electric current.
items.explanation: Chemical processes release energy from food for cellular activities.

items.truth: A battery stores energy chemically.
items.lie: A battery stores its energy as a tank of moving electrons.
items.explanation: Chemical reactions in the battery transfer energy to charges in a circuit.

items.truth: In an ideal falling system, gravitational potential energy can become kinetic energy.
items.lie: An ideal falling object gains kinetic energy without any other energy change.
items.explanation: As height falls, gravitational potential energy decreases while kinetic energy increases.

items.truth: Mechanical energy can decrease while total energy remains conserved.
items.lie: If mechanical energy decreases, total energy must have been destroyed.
items.explanation: Mechanical energy can transfer to internal energy through friction or drag.

items.truth: Heating transfers energy because of a temperature difference.
items.lie: Heating transfers a substance called cold from cooler objects into warmer objects.
items.explanation: Heat is energy in transfer; cold is not a material substance.

items.truth: Net thermal energy transfer occurs from hotter to cooler objects without external work.
items.lie: Net thermal energy transfer naturally runs from cooler to hotter objects without external work.
items.explanation: The spontaneous net transfer is down the temperature difference.

items.truth: Temperature and total internal energy are different quantities.
items.lie: Two objects at the same temperature must contain the same total internal energy.
items.explanation: Internal energy depends on amount and type of matter as well as temperature and state.

items.truth: Thermal conduction can occur through a solid without the solid moving as a whole.
items.lie: Thermal conduction requires the entire solid to flow from hot to cold.
items.explanation: Energy is transferred through microscopic interactions rather than bulk flow.

items.truth: Convection involves bulk movement of a fluid.
items.lie: Convection is the main heat-transfer process within a rigid solid.
items.explanation: Convection requires fluid motion, as in liquids and gases.

items.truth: Thermal radiation can transfer energy through empty space.
items.lie: Thermal radiation needs air particles to carry energy.
items.explanation: Electromagnetic radiation can travel through a vacuum.

items.truth: Insulation reduces the rate of thermal energy transfer.
items.lie: Insulation creates thermal energy to keep an object warm.
items.explanation: Insulation slows energy transfer; it is not an energy source.

items.truth: Efficiency compares useful output energy with input energy.
items.lie: Efficiency is calculated by dividing input energy by useful output energy.
items.explanation: Efficiency = useful output ÷ input, often expressed as a percentage.

items.truth: A machine with 80 J useful output from 100 J input is 80% efficient.
items.lie: A machine with 80 J useful output from 100 J input is 125% efficient.

items.truth: An ordinary machine cannot deliver more total energy than it receives and releases from storage.
items.lie: An ordinary machine can continuously create extra energy if its gears are arranged correctly.
items.explanation: Energy conservation rules out a machine that produces energy from nothing.

items.truth: A kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy.
items.lie: A kilowatt-hour is a unit of power.
items.explanation: Power multiplied by time gives energy; 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ.

items.truth: Solar panels can convert incoming light energy to electrical energy.
items.lie: Solar panels create energy from nothing when sunlight reaches them.
items.explanation: The light supplies energy that the panels convert.

items.truth: Wind turbines obtain energy from moving air.
items.lie: Wind turbines produce energy by consuming the air itself.
items.explanation: Moving air has kinetic energy; the turbine transfers some of it.

items.truth: Doing work on an object can change its energy.
items.lie: Mechanical work can never transfer energy to an object.
items.explanation: A force acting through a displacement can transfer energy mechanically.

items.truth: Energy can be transferred between objects.
items.lie: Energy cannot be transferred between objects.
items.explanation: Heating, mechanical work and radiation can transfer energy. Energy is conserved overall.

items.truth: A stretched spring can store elastic potential energy.
items.lie: A stretched spring cannot store energy until it starts moving.
items.explanation: Elastic potential energy is associated with deformation. A stationary stretched spring can store it.

items.truth: Sound needs a medium through which to travel.
items.lie: Sound can travel through a vacuum.
items.explanation: Sound is a mechanical disturbance transmitted through matter. A vacuum has no particles to transmit it.

items.truth: Increasing a sound wave’s frequency increases its pitch.
items.lie: Increasing a sound wave’s amplitude increases its pitch.
items.explanation: Pitch relates primarily to frequency. Amplitude relates to the strength of pressure variations and perceived loudness.

items.truth: Waves can transfer energy without transporting matter over the whole journey.
items.lie: A wave must carry the same particles all the way from its source to its destination.
items.explanation: In many waves, particles oscillate locally while the disturbance travels.

items.truth: Wavelength is the distance between successive points in the same phase.
items.lie: Wavelength is the time required for one oscillation.
items.explanation: Wavelength is a distance; period is a time.

items.truth: Frequency is the number of oscillations per second.
items.lie: Frequency is the distance a wave travels in one second.
items.explanation: Frequency counts cycles per second; wave speed measures travel distance per second.

items.truth: Frequency is measured in hertz.
items.lie: Frequency is measured in metres.
items.explanation: One hertz is one cycle per second.

items.truth: The period is the time taken for one complete oscillation.
items.lie: The period is the number of oscillations in one second.
items.explanation: Period measures time per cycle; frequency counts cycles per time.

items.truth: Doubling frequency halves the period.
items.lie: Doubling frequency doubles the period.
items.explanation: Period and frequency are reciprocals: T = 1/f.

items.truth: A wave with frequency 5 Hz has a period of 0.2 s.
items.lie: A wave with frequency 5 Hz has a period of 5 s.

items.truth: Wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength.
items.lie: Wave speed equals frequency divided by wavelength.
items.explanation: v = fλ, with units of metres per second.

items.truth: A wave with wavelength 2 m and frequency 3 Hz travels at 6 m/s.
items.lie: A wave with wavelength 2 m and frequency 3 Hz travels at 1.5 m/s.
items.explanation: Multiply frequency by wavelength: 3 × 2 = 6.

items.truth: At fixed wave speed, increasing frequency decreases wavelength.
items.lie: At fixed wave speed, increasing frequency increases wavelength.
items.explanation: Because v = fλ is fixed, wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency.

items.truth: Amplitude is maximum displacement from equilibrium.
items.lie: Amplitude is the distance between a crest and the adjacent trough.
items.explanation: Crest-to-trough displacement is twice the amplitude for a symmetric wave.

items.truth: In a transverse wave, oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of travel.
items.lie: In a transverse wave, oscillations are parallel to the direction of travel.
items.explanation: Transverse motion is across the propagation direction.

items.truth: In a longitudinal wave, oscillations are parallel to the direction of travel.
items.lie: In a longitudinal wave, oscillations are always perpendicular to the direction of travel.
items.explanation: Longitudinal oscillations occur along the propagation direction.

items.truth: Sound in air is a longitudinal wave.
items.lie: Sound in air is a transverse wave.
items.explanation: Air undergoes pressure variations through compressions and rarefactions along the travel direction.

items.truth: A compression in a sound wave has higher pressure than the adjacent rarefaction.
items.lie: A compression in a sound wave has lower pressure than the adjacent rarefaction.
items.explanation: Particles are more crowded in a compression, giving higher local pressure.

items.truth: An echo is reflected sound.
items.lie: An echo is sound that has stopped moving permanently.
items.explanation: Sound reflects from a surface and can return to the listener after a delay.

items.truth: For an echo, sound travels to the reflector and back.
items.lie: For an echo, the recorded time includes only the outward journey.
items.explanation: The round trip is twice the source-to-reflector distance when the source and receiver are together.

items.truth: Sound generally travels faster in steel than in air.
items.lie: Sound always travels faster in air than in solids.
items.explanation: Wave speed depends on the material’s stiffness and density; steel transmits sound much faster than air.

items.truth: Increasing air temperature generally increases the speed of sound in air.
items.lie: Increasing air temperature generally decreases the speed of sound in air.
items.explanation: Within ordinary classroom conditions, sound speed increases with air temperature.

items.truth: Changing sound amplitude does not by itself change its frequency.
items.lie: Making a sound wave larger in amplitude necessarily raises its frequency.
items.explanation: Amplitude and frequency are separate wave properties.

items.truth: A louder sound does not necessarily have a higher pitch.
items.lie: A louder sound must have a higher pitch.
items.explanation: Loudness relates to intensity and hearing; pitch relates primarily to frequency.

items.truth: When a wave crosses into another stationary medium, its frequency is set by the source.
items.lie: When a wave crosses into another stationary medium, its frequency must change.
items.explanation: Speed and wavelength can change at the boundary while frequency remains the same.

items.truth: Diffraction is the spreading of waves around edges or through gaps.
items.lie: Diffraction is the complete disappearance of waves at every gap.
items.explanation: Waves spread, especially when the gap size is comparable to wavelength.

items.truth: Overlapping waves can produce constructive interference.
items.lie: Overlapping waves always cancel each other completely.
items.explanation: Their displacements add; the result depends on their relative phases.

items.truth: Destructive interference can reduce the resultant displacement.
items.lie: Destructive interference means both sources have stopped producing waves.
items.explanation: Opposite displacements can cancel locally while the waves continue to exist.

items.truth: A standing-wave node has zero displacement in the ideal pattern.
items.lie: A standing-wave node has the largest displacement in the ideal pattern.
items.explanation: Nodes are stationary points; antinodes have maximum amplitude.

items.truth: A source approaching a stationary listener can be heard at a higher frequency.
items.lie: A source approaching a stationary listener is always heard at a lower frequency.
items.explanation: The Doppler effect compresses the spacing of arriving wavefronts for an approaching source.

items.truth: Ultrasound has a frequency above the upper limit of ordinary human hearing.
items.lie: Ultrasound is sound with a frequency below ordinary human hearing.
items.explanation: Ultrasound is conventionally above 20 kHz; very low-frequency sound is infrasound.

items.truth: Light is an electromagnetic wave.
items.lie: Light is a mechanical pressure wave in air.
items.explanation: Light involves electromagnetic fields rather than sound-like pressure variations.

items.truth: Visible light is only part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
items.lie: All electromagnetic radiation is visible to human eyes.
items.explanation: Radio, infrared, ultraviolet and other bands lie outside human visible vision.

items.truth: In a vacuum, all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed.
items.lie: In a vacuum, radio waves travel much slower than visible light.
items.explanation: All electromagnetic waves have the same vacuum speed, c.

items.truth: Light travels much faster than sound in air.
items.lie: Sound in air travels faster than light in a vacuum.
items.explanation: Light travels about 300 million m/s; sound in ordinary air travels a few hundred m/s.

items.truth: A light-year measures distance.
items.lie: A light-year measures the age of a star.
items.explanation: It is the distance light travels in one year.

items.truth: We see an ordinary non-luminous object when light from it enters our eyes.
items.lie: Our eyes see ordinary objects by sending out beams of light.
items.explanation: Light reflected or scattered from the object reaches the eye.

items.truth: A luminous object emits light.
items.lie: A luminous object can only reflect light from other objects.
items.explanation: Stars and glowing lamps produce light; an illuminated book mainly reflects it.

items.truth: In a uniform transparent medium, light rays travel in straight lines.
items.lie: In a uniform transparent medium, light rays always curve around opaque objects.
items.explanation: The straight-ray model explains ordinary shadows and ray diagrams.

items.truth: An opaque object can block light and form a shadow.
items.lie: An opaque object transmits all incoming visible light.
items.explanation: Opaque materials do not transmit visible light through their bulk in this model.

items.truth: At a mirror, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
items.lie: At a mirror, the angle of reflection is always twice the angle of incidence.
items.explanation: Both angles are measured from the normal to the surface.

items.truth: Reflection angles are measured from the normal.
items.lie: Reflection angles in the usual law are measured from the mirror surface.
items.explanation: The normal is perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray strikes.

items.truth: A plane mirror forms a virtual image behind the mirror.
items.lie: A plane mirror forms a real image that can be caught on a screen behind it.
items.explanation: Reflected rays appear to come from behind the mirror but do not actually converge there.

items.truth: An object’s image in a plane mirror is the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.
items.lie: An object’s image in a plane mirror is always twice as far behind it as the object is in front.
items.explanation: The perpendicular object and image distances are equal.

items.truth: Refraction can change the direction of light crossing between media.
items.lie: Refraction means light bounces back into the medium it came from.
items.explanation: Refraction involves transmission with a speed change; bouncing back is reflection.

items.truth: Light entering glass from air at an oblique angle usually bends towards the normal.
items.lie: Light entering glass from air at an oblique angle usually bends away from the normal.
items.explanation: Light slows in ordinary glass and bends towards the normal.

items.truth: A ray entering glass along the normal can change speed without changing direction.
items.lie: A ray entering glass along the normal must turn through a non-zero angle.
items.explanation: At normal incidence there is no bending, even though speed changes.

items.truth: A straw in water can appear bent because of refraction.
items.lie: A straw appears bent in water because the water necessarily bends the straw physically.
items.explanation: Light from the submerged part changes direction as it passes into air.

items.truth: A prism can separate white light into colours.
items.lie: A prism creates all visible colours from a single-frequency beam.
items.explanation: Different wavelengths refract by different amounts; white light already contains a range of wavelengths.

items.truth: Red visible light has a longer wavelength than violet visible light.
items.lie: Red visible light has a shorter wavelength than violet visible light.
items.explanation: Visible wavelengths decrease from red towards violet.

items.truth: Violet visible light has a higher frequency than red visible light.
items.lie: Violet visible light has a lower frequency than red visible light.
items.explanation: At the same wave speed, shorter wavelength means higher frequency.

items.truth: An ordinary convex glass lens in air can converge parallel light rays.
items.lie: An ordinary convex glass lens in air always spreads parallel light rays apart.
items.explanation: A converging lens brings parallel rays towards a focus.

items.truth: An ordinary concave glass lens in air diverges parallel light rays.
items.lie: An ordinary concave glass lens in air brings parallel light rays to a real focus.
items.explanation: A diverging lens spreads rays so they appear to come from a virtual focus.

items.truth: A red object under white light reflects some red wavelengths towards the observer.
items.lie: A red object looks red because it absorbs all red light reaching it.
items.explanation: The light reaching the observer includes reflected red wavelengths; other wavelengths may be absorbed.

items.truth: Black surfaces generally absorb more visible light than white surfaces under the same illumination.
items.lie: Black surfaces look black because they reflect all visible wavelengths strongly.
items.explanation: Low visible reflection makes a surface appear dark.

items.truth: Adding red, green and blue light in suitable proportions can produce white light.
items.lie: Mixing red, green and blue light necessarily produces black light.
items.explanation: Additive colour mixing combines light; it differs from mixing paints.

items.truth: Total internal reflection requires light to travel towards a lower-refractive-index medium at a sufficiently large angle.
items.lie: Total internal reflection occurs at every boundary and every angle.
items.explanation: It requires the appropriate index change and an incidence angle greater than the critical angle.

items.truth: Optical fibres can guide light using total internal reflection.
items.lie: Optical fibres guide light because light travels only in metal wires.
items.explanation: Light is confined by the fibre’s optical structure, commonly through total internal reflection.

items.truth: Ultraviolet radiation is outside the visible range for humans.
items.lie: Ultraviolet radiation is simply very bright purple light that humans can always see.
items.explanation: Ultraviolet wavelengths are shorter than the visible violet end of the spectrum.

items.truth: Light can travel through a vacuum.
items.lie: Light needs air in order to travel.
items.explanation: Light is an electromagnetic wave and does not require a material medium. Sunlight reaches Earth through space.

items.truth: Doubling the distance from an ideal point light source reduces irradiance to one quarter.
items.lie: Doubling the distance from an ideal point light source reduces irradiance to one half.
items.explanation: For an isotropic point source without absorption, irradiance follows an inverse-square relationship: E ∝ 1/r².

items.truth: Like electric charges repel each other.
items.lie: Like electric charges attract each other.
items.explanation: Charges of the same sign repel; opposite signs attract.

items.truth: Unlike electric charges attract each other.
items.lie: Unlike electric charges repel each other.
items.explanation: A positive and a negative charge attract.

items.truth: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
items.lie: A neutral atom contains no charged particles.
items.explanation: Its positive and negative charges balance rather than being absent.

items.truth: An object with excess electrons is negatively charged.
items.lie: An object with excess electrons is positively charged.
items.explanation: Electrons carry negative charge.

items.truth: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge.
items.lie: Electric current is the amount of energy stored in a circuit.
items.explanation: Current measures charge passing per unit time.

items.truth: The SI unit of current is the ampere.
items.lie: The SI unit of current is the volt.
items.explanation: Amperes measure current; volts measure potential difference.

items.truth: Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge.
items.lie: Potential difference is charge transferred per unit time.
items.explanation: Voltage measures joules per coulomb; current measures coulombs per second.

items.truth: Electrical resistance is measured in ohms.
items.lie: Electrical resistance is measured in amperes.
items.explanation: The ohm is the SI resistance unit.

items.truth: An ammeter is normally connected in series with the component whose current is measured.
items.lie: An ammeter is normally connected directly across a power supply to measure a component’s current.
items.explanation: Series connection lets the component’s current pass through the ammeter; an across-supply connection can short the supply.

items.truth: A voltmeter is connected across a component to measure its potential difference.
items.lie: A voltmeter must replace the component to measure its potential difference.
items.explanation: Parallel connection compares the potentials at the component’s two terminals.

items.truth: A simple circuit needs a complete conducting path for a steady current.
items.lie: A single disconnected wire from a battery provides a complete path for steady current.
items.explanation: A closed loop is required for sustained current in a simple battery circuit.

items.truth: An open switch breaks the conducting path.
items.lie: An open switch completes the conducting path.
items.explanation: Opening separates the contacts and interrupts the loop.

items.truth: In a simple series circuit, current is the same through each component.
items.lie: In a simple series circuit, each component uses up some current.
items.explanation: Charge is conserved; energy is transferred but current is not progressively consumed.

items.truth: For resistors in series, total resistance is the sum of their resistances.
items.lie: For resistors in series, total resistance is smaller than every individual resistance.
items.explanation: Series resistances add because the same current crosses each potential drop.

items.truth: Adding a resistor in series to a fixed-voltage supply reduces the current.
items.lie: Adding a resistor in series to a fixed-voltage supply increases the current.
items.explanation: Total resistance rises, so I = V/R falls.

items.truth: Parallel branches share the same potential difference between their common endpoints.
items.lie: Parallel branches must share the same current regardless of their resistances.
items.explanation: Voltage is common; branch current depends on branch resistance.

items.truth: At a circuit junction, total current entering equals total current leaving in steady conditions.
items.lie: A circuit junction creates extra current when a wire splits into two branches.
items.explanation: Charge conservation requires the incoming and outgoing currents to balance.

items.truth: For an ohmic resistor at constant temperature, current is proportional to potential difference.
items.lie: For an ohmic resistor at constant temperature, doubling voltage halves current.
items.explanation: With constant resistance, I = V/R.

items.truth: A 6 V potential difference across a 3 Ω resistor produces a 2 A current.
items.lie: A 6 V potential difference across a 3 Ω resistor produces an 18 A current.

items.truth: A component carrying 2 A across 6 V transfers electrical energy at 12 W.
items.lie: A component carrying 2 A across 6 V transfers electrical energy at 3 W.

items.truth: Conventional current is opposite to electron drift in a metal wire.
items.lie: Conventional current is defined as the direction of electron drift in a metal wire.
items.explanation: Conventional current follows the direction positive charge would move.

items.truth: Metals generally conduct electricity well because they contain mobile electrons.
items.lie: Metals conduct electricity because all their protons move freely between atoms.
items.explanation: Conduction electrons are mobile; metal ions form the lattice.

items.truth: An electrical insulator resists charge movement through its bulk.
items.lie: An electrical insulator contains no electrons.
items.explanation: Insulators contain electrons but do not provide freely moving charges as metals do.

items.truth: Rubbing two suitable materials can transfer electrons between them.
items.lie: Rubbing two materials creates positive and negative charge from nothing.
items.explanation: Charge is transferred and separated; total charge is conserved.

items.truth: Earthing can let electrons move between an object and Earth.
items.lie: Earthing always adds protons to a charged object.
items.explanation: Electrons can enter or leave through a conducting path; protons do not flow through the wire.

items.truth: A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field.
items.lie: A wire can produce a magnetic field only if it is made from iron.
items.explanation: Electric current produces a magnetic field even in non-ferromagnetic conductors.

items.truth: Reversing the current in a solenoid reverses its magnetic poles.
items.lie: Reversing the current in a solenoid leaves its magnetic poles unchanged.
items.explanation: The field direction follows current direction through the coil.

items.truth: Increasing current in an ideal air-core solenoid increases its magnetic field magnitude.
items.lie: Increasing current in an ideal air-core solenoid reduces its magnetic field magnitude.
items.explanation: For fixed coil geometry, magnetic field is proportional to current.

items.truth: Electric current in a metal wire involves moving electrons.
items.lie: Electric current in a metal wire requires protons to travel along the wire.
items.explanation: Conduction electrons move through the metal. The positive ions remain in the lattice rather than flowing along the wire.

items.truth: A nearby charged object can redistribute charge in a neutral conductor without touching it.
items.lie: A nearby charged object cannot affect charge distribution in a conductor unless it touches it.
items.explanation: Electrostatic induction redistributes mobile electrons. This does not by itself change the conductor’s total charge.

items.truth: An element contains atoms with the same proton number.
items.lie: An element contains atoms that all have the same neutron number.
items.explanation: Proton number defines the element; neutron number can vary between isotopes.

items.truth: A compound contains elements chemically combined in a definite ratio.
items.lie: A compound is any mixture of substances in any ratio.
items.explanation: Compounds have chemically bonded constituents and defined composition; mixtures can vary.

items.truth: Air is a mixture of gases.
items.lie: Air is a single pure compound.
items.explanation: Air contains nitrogen, oxygen and other gases that are not all chemically bonded together.

items.truth: A molecule can contain atoms of just one element.
items.lie: Every molecule must contain at least two different elements.
items.explanation: An oxygen molecule, O₂, contains two oxygen atoms and only one element.

items.truth: A water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
items.lie: A water molecule contains two oxygen atoms and one hydrogen atom.
items.explanation: The formula H₂O specifies the numbers of each atom.

items.truth: Isotopes of an element have different numbers of neutrons.
items.lie: Isotopes of an element have different numbers of protons.
items.explanation: Isotopes retain the same atomic number but differ in mass number.

items.truth: An atom’s mass number is its number of protons plus neutrons.
items.lie: An atom’s mass number is its number of protons plus electrons.
items.explanation: Mass number counts nucleons in the nucleus.

items.truth: Most of an atom’s mass is in its nucleus.
items.lie: Most of an atom’s mass is in its electrons.
items.explanation: Protons and neutrons are much more massive than electrons.

items.truth: A proton has positive electric charge.
items.lie: A neutron has positive electric charge.
items.explanation: Protons are positive, electrons negative and neutrons electrically neutral.

items.truth: Atoms in a solid continue to move microscopically.
items.lie: Particles in a solid are completely motionless.
items.explanation: Particles vibrate around positions even though the solid keeps its overall shape.

items.truth: A gas expands to fill its container.
items.lie: A gas has a fixed shape independent of its container.
items.explanation: Gas particles move freely and spread through the available volume.

items.truth: A liquid has a fairly fixed volume but takes the shape of its container.
items.lie: A liquid has a fixed shape but no fixed volume.
items.explanation: Liquids can flow, while their particles remain close together.

items.truth: Melting is a physical change.
items.lie: Melting a pure substance necessarily makes a new chemical substance.
items.explanation: A change of state changes arrangement and motion rather than chemical identity.

items.truth: Condensation changes a gas into a liquid.
items.lie: Condensation changes a liquid into a gas.
items.explanation: Gas-to-liquid change is condensation; liquid-to-gas change is vaporisation.

items.truth: Freezing changes a liquid into a solid.
items.lie: Freezing changes a solid into a liquid.
items.explanation: Liquid-to-solid change is freezing; solid-to-liquid change is melting.

items.truth: A saturated solution contains the maximum equilibrium amount of dissolved solute under the stated conditions.
items.lie: A saturated solution contains no dissolved solute.
items.explanation: At saturation, no more of that solute dissolves at equilibrium without changing conditions.

items.truth: Filtration can separate insoluble sand from water.
items.lie: Ordinary filter paper can remove dissolved salt from salt water.
items.explanation: Sand particles are retained; dissolved ions pass through with the water.

items.truth: Evaporating water from salt water can leave solid salt behind.
items.lie: Evaporating water from salt water necessarily evaporates the salt at the same rate.
items.explanation: Under ordinary evaporation conditions the water leaves as vapour while the non-volatile salt remains.

items.truth: Distillation can separate substances using differences in volatility.
items.lie: Distillation separates substances only by particle size.
items.explanation: Vaporisation followed by condensation uses differences in how readily substances vaporise.

items.truth: Mass is conserved in an ordinary chemical reaction in a closed system.
items.lie: An ordinary chemical reaction in a closed system must reduce total mass.
items.explanation: Atoms are conserved; apparent losses often involve gases escaping from an open system.

items.truth: A catalyst can increase reaction rate without being consumed overall.
items.lie: A catalyst increases reaction rate by being permanently used up as a reactant.
items.explanation: A catalyst participates in a pathway and is regenerated overall.

items.truth: Increasing temperature often increases reaction rate.
items.lie: Increasing temperature always stops reacting particles from colliding.
items.explanation: Higher temperature commonly increases collision frequency and the fraction of collisions with sufficient energy.

items.truth: A smaller particle size can increase the reaction rate of a solid by exposing more surface area.
items.lie: Breaking a solid into smaller pieces always reduces its exposed surface area.
items.explanation: More exposed surface allows more contact with other reactants.

items.truth: In a balanced chemical equation, coefficients can change but substance formulae stay fixed.
items.lie: Balancing a chemical equation requires changing the subscripts inside substance formulae.
items.explanation: Changing a subscript changes the substance; coefficients change the number of units reacting.

items.truth: At 25°C, a neutral aqueous solution has pH 7.
items.lie: At 25°C, a neutral aqueous solution has pH 0.
items.explanation: Neutral water has equal hydrogen and hydroxide ion concentrations; at 25°C this corresponds to pH 7.

items.truth: An atom that loses an electron becomes a positive ion.
items.lie: An atom that loses an electron becomes a negative ion.
items.explanation: Losing negatively charged electrons leaves more protons than electrons, giving a net positive charge.

items.truth: The number of protons determines an atom’s element.
items.lie: The number of neutrons determines an atom’s element.
items.explanation: Atomic number is the number of protons. Atoms of the same element can have different neutron numbers: these are isotopes.

items.truth: Atoms are conserved and rearranged in an ordinary chemical reaction.
items.lie: An ordinary chemical reaction creates new atoms from nothing.
items.explanation: In ordinary chemical reactions, atoms are rearranged into new combinations. Balanced equations conserve the number of atoms of each element.

items.truth: Evaporation can occur below a liquid’s boiling point.
items.lie: Evaporation occurs only when a liquid reaches its boiling point.
items.explanation: Some surface particles can escape at temperatures below boiling. Boiling occurs throughout the liquid under suitable pressure conditions.

items.truth: A dissolved substance can remain present even when it is no longer visible.
items.lie: A substance ceases to exist when it dissolves and becomes invisible.
items.explanation: Solute particles disperse through the solvent. Dissolving does not mean the substance has vanished.

items.truth: The cell membrane controls movement of many substances into and out of a cell.
items.lie: The cell membrane allows every substance to cross equally freely.
items.explanation: Membranes are selectively permeable, with transport depending on molecules and membrane proteins.

items.truth: Cytoplasm contains the fluid environment in which many cell reactions occur.
items.lie: Cytoplasm is found only outside the cell membrane.
items.explanation: Cytoplasm lies within the cell membrane and supports cellular processes.

items.truth: DNA carries hereditary information.
items.lie: DNA’s main role is to digest food outside cells.
items.explanation: DNA stores information used in inheritance and in producing cell components.

items.truth: The nucleus of a typical eukaryotic cell contains most of its DNA.
items.lie: The nucleus of a typical eukaryotic cell contains no DNA.
items.explanation: Chromosomes in the nucleus contain most eukaryotic genetic material; some organelles also contain DNA.

items.truth: Bacteria are prokaryotic organisms.
items.lie: Bacteria are tiny animals with membrane-bound nuclei.
items.explanation: Bacteria lack a membrane-bound nucleus and are not animals.

items.truth: A plant cell usually has a cell wall outside its membrane.
items.lie: A plant cell has a cell wall instead of a cell membrane.
items.explanation: Plant cells have both a membrane and a surrounding wall.

items.truth: Animal cells do not have cellulose cell walls.
items.lie: Animal cells have the same cellulose walls as plant cells.
items.explanation: Animal cells have membranes but lack the cellulose walls typical of plants.

items.truth: Chloroplasts are sites of photosynthesis in plant cells.
items.lie: Chloroplasts are the main sites of cellular respiration in plant cells.
items.explanation: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts; much aerobic respiration occurs in mitochondria.

items.truth: Not every plant cell contains chloroplasts.
items.lie: Every plant cell contains chloroplasts, including all root cells.
items.explanation: Many non-photosynthetic plant cells, such as typical root cells, lack chloroplasts.

items.truth: Mitochondria occur in both plant and animal cells.
items.lie: Mitochondria occur only in animal cells.
items.explanation: Both groups use mitochondria in aerobic cellular respiration.

items.truth: Ribosomes make proteins.
items.lie: Ribosomes store all the cell’s hereditary information.
items.explanation: Ribosomes assemble amino acids into proteins using genetic instructions.

items.truth: A large central vacuole helps support many plant cells.
items.lie: A plant cell’s central vacuole is always an empty air space.
items.explanation: The vacuole contains fluid; water uptake contributes to turgor pressure.

items.truth: Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient.
items.lie: Diffusion is net movement from lower to higher concentration without energy input.
items.explanation: Random motion produces a net spread from higher to lower concentration.

items.truth: Diffusion can occur without a living cell being present.
items.lie: Diffusion can occur only inside living cells.
items.explanation: Particles can diffuse in solutions and gases independently of life.

items.truth: Osmosis involves net water movement across a selectively permeable membrane.
items.lie: Osmosis is the movement of any solute through any barrier.
items.explanation: Osmosis concerns water moving across a membrane in response to a water-potential difference.

items.truth: In the usual dilute-solution model, water moves by osmosis towards the side with greater solute concentration if the solute cannot cross.
items.lie: In the usual dilute-solution model, water moves by osmosis towards the side with lower solute concentration if the solute cannot cross.
items.explanation: With other conditions equal, greater dissolved-solute concentration lowers water potential.

items.truth: Active transport can move substances against a concentration gradient using energy.
items.lie: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient without requiring energy.
items.explanation: Transport against a gradient requires an energy source and appropriate transport machinery.

items.truth: A specialised cell’s structure can help it carry out its function.
items.lie: All cells must have identical shapes to perform different functions.
items.explanation: Features such as surface area, shape and organelle abundance can support particular jobs.

items.truth: Root hair cells have extensions that increase their absorbing surface area.
items.lie: Root hair extensions reduce the surface available for absorption.
items.explanation: The extensions increase contact with the soil solution.

items.truth: Mature human red blood cells lack a nucleus.
items.lie: Every mature human red blood cell has a large nucleus.
items.explanation: Human red blood cells lose their nucleus during development, leaving more room for haemoglobin.

items.truth: A tissue is a group of cells working together in a function.
items.lie: A tissue is a collection of unrelated organs.
items.explanation: Cells form tissues; tissues combine into organs.

items.truth: An organ contains multiple tissue types.
items.lie: Every organ consists of just one cell.
items.explanation: An organ is a structure with different tissues working together.

items.truth: Unicellular organisms carry out life processes within one cell.
items.lie: A unicellular organism cannot carry out life processes because it has only one cell.
items.explanation: One cell can perform the functions needed by the organism.

items.truth: Multicellular organisms contain many cells.
items.lie: Multicellular means that an organism contains many nuclei but only one cell.
items.explanation: Multicellularity refers to the presence of multiple cells.

items.truth: In mitosis, a eukaryotic cell normally produces two genetically equivalent daughter nuclei.
items.lie: In mitosis, a eukaryotic cell normally produces four daughter nuclei with half the chromosome number.
items.explanation: Mitosis preserves chromosome number; meiosis is the division associated with chromosome-number reduction.

items.truth: Cells normally copy their DNA before mitotic division.
items.lie: Cells normally copy their DNA only after both daughter cells have separated.
items.explanation: DNA replication before division allows daughter cells to receive genetic information.

items.truth: A microscope’s magnification and resolution are different properties.
items.lie: Increasing magnification always reveals more detail, even if resolution stays unchanged.
items.explanation: Magnification enlarges the image; resolution limits how close features can be distinguished.

items.truth: Total magnification of a light microscope is eyepiece magnification multiplied by objective magnification.
items.lie: Total magnification of a light microscope is eyepiece magnification added to objective magnification.
items.explanation: A 10× eyepiece and 40× objective give 400× total magnification.

items.truth: Plant cells carry out cellular respiration.
items.lie: Plant cells carry out photosynthesis instead of cellular respiration.
items.explanation: Plants need usable energy for cell processes. They carry out respiration as well as photosynthesis in photosynthetic tissues.

items.truth: Not all cells have a nucleus.
items.lie: Every cell has a nucleus.
items.explanation: Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Some specialised eukaryotic cells also lack one.

items.truth: A population consists of members of one species in an area.
items.lie: A population consists of all species in an area.
items.explanation: All the populations together form a community.

items.truth: A community includes populations of different species.
items.lie: A community contains only non-living environmental factors.
items.explanation: Communities are the living component, containing interacting populations.

items.truth: An ecosystem includes living organisms and their non-living surroundings.
items.lie: An ecosystem includes living organisms but excludes water, light and soil conditions.
items.explanation: Biotic and abiotic components interact in an ecosystem.

items.truth: Abiotic factors are non-living environmental components.
items.lie: Predators are abiotic factors because they affect other organisms.
items.explanation: Predators are living, so they are biotic factors.

items.truth: Temperature is an abiotic factor.
items.lie: Temperature is a biotic factor.
items.explanation: Temperature is a physical condition, not a living organism.

items.truth: A habitat is the place where an organism lives.
items.lie: A habitat is the organism’s position in a food chain only.
items.explanation: Habitat describes where it lives; feeding role is only part of its ecological niche.

items.truth: Producers make organic substances using energy from light or chemical reactions.
items.lie: Producers obtain all their organic food by eating other organisms.
items.explanation: Plants use photosynthesis, while some microbes use chemical energy.

items.truth: Consumers obtain organic material by feeding on other organisms or their products.
items.lie: Consumers make all their food directly from sunlight.
items.explanation: Consumers depend on existing organic material.

items.truth: An herbivore feeds on plant material.
items.lie: An herbivore feeds exclusively on animals.
items.explanation: Herbivores consume producers such as plants; carnivores consume animals.

items.truth: An omnivore can eat both plant and animal material.
items.lie: An omnivore can eat only one type of plant.
items.explanation: Omnivores use both plant and animal food sources.

items.truth: Food-chain arrows usually point in the direction of energy transfer.
items.lie: Food-chain arrows usually point from the predator to the prey it eats.
items.explanation: The arrow goes from the food organism to the consumer receiving energy.

items.truth: A food web shows multiple feeding relationships.
items.lie: A food web shows that each species has exactly one food source.
items.explanation: Food webs connect many food chains and allow several links per species.

items.truth: A species can occupy more than one trophic level in a food web.
items.lie: A species must occupy exactly one trophic level regardless of its diet.
items.explanation: An omnivore can feed at different levels by eating both plants and animals.

items.truth: Not all energy eaten by a consumer becomes new consumer biomass.
items.lie: All energy eaten by a consumer becomes new consumer biomass.
items.explanation: Energy is used in respiration, transferred as heat and lost in waste or uneaten material.

items.truth: The percentage of energy transferred between trophic levels varies.
items.lie: Exactly 10% of energy is transferred at every feeding link in every ecosystem.
items.explanation: Ten per cent is a useful rough guide, not a universal fixed value.

items.truth: Competition can occur between members of the same species.
items.lie: Competition occurs only between different species.
items.explanation: Individuals of one species may compete for food, space or mates.

items.truth: Competition can occur when organisms share a limited resource.
items.lie: Competition requires organisms to physically fight each other.
items.explanation: Resources can be depleted without direct physical contact.

items.truth: Predation involves one organism feeding on another after capturing it.
items.lie: Predation always benefits both the predator and its prey.
items.explanation: The predator benefits while the prey is harmed.

items.truth: In mutualism, both interacting species benefit.
items.lie: In mutualism, one species benefits and the other is always harmed.
items.explanation: Mutualism is a positive interaction for both partners.

items.truth: A parasite benefits at the expense of its host.
items.lie: A parasite always improves its host’s health.
items.explanation: Parasitism benefits the parasite and harms the host.

items.truth: Carrying capacity depends on environmental conditions and resources.
items.lie: Carrying capacity is a fixed number that can never change.
items.explanation: Food, space, water and other conditions can change the population an environment supports.

items.truth: Population size can change through births, deaths, immigration and emigration.
items.lie: Population size can change only through births and deaths.
items.explanation: Movement into and out of an area also changes population size.

items.truth: A quadrat can be used to sample plants in a habitat.
items.lie: A quadrat is usually the best method for counting fast-flying birds directly.
items.explanation: Quadrats suit stationary or slow-moving organisms; mobile animals often need other methods.

items.truth: Random sampling helps reduce selection bias.
items.lie: Choosing only the most interesting-looking sampling sites guarantees an unbiased estimate.
items.explanation: Random selection reduces deliberate or unconscious preference for particular sites.

items.truth: A transect can show changes in organisms along an environmental gradient.
items.lie: A transect must sample only one isolated point.
items.explanation: Sampling along a line can reveal spatial patterns.

items.truth: Biodiversity includes variation within species, between species and among ecosystems.
items.lie: Biodiversity refers only to the number of animals in an area.
items.explanation: Biodiversity includes genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.

items.truth: An introduced species can alter a food web.
items.lie: An introduced species can never affect native species if it is small.
items.explanation: Introduced organisms may compete, prey, spread disease or change habitat regardless of size.

items.truth: Removing a predator can have indirect effects on other parts of a food web.
items.lie: Removing a predator can affect only that predator and no other species.
items.explanation: Changes can spread through feeding interactions and produce trophic cascades.

items.truth: Energy flows through food chains and is transferred to the surroundings.
items.lie: Energy is endlessly recycled within a food chain without transfer to the surroundings.
items.explanation: Energy enters ecosystems and is transferred, with much eventually dissipated as heat. Matter cycles; energy flows.

items.truth: Decomposers help recycle nutrients in ecosystems.
items.lie: Decomposers prevent nutrients from being recycled in ecosystems.
items.explanation: Decomposers break down organic material, returning nutrients to forms that can be used again.

items.truth: Earth’s rotation produces the regular cycle of day and night.
items.lie: Earth’s yearly orbit around the Sun produces each day and night.
items.explanation: Rotation turns different parts of Earth towards or away from sunlight.

items.truth: Earth takes about one year to orbit the Sun.
items.lie: Earth takes about one day to orbit the Sun.
items.explanation: One day describes roughly one rotation; one year describes one orbit.

items.truth: The Moon shines mainly by reflecting sunlight.
items.lie: The Moon produces its own visible light through nuclear fusion.
items.explanation: The Moon is not a star; sunlight reflected from its surface reaches us.

items.truth: A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon blocks our view of the Sun.
items.lie: A solar eclipse occurs when Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon.
items.explanation: The Moon lies between Sun and observer during a solar eclipse.

items.truth: A lunar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes through Earth’s shadow.
items.lie: A lunar eclipse occurs when the Sun passes through the Moon’s shadow.
items.explanation: Earth lies between Sun and Moon and blocks some sunlight reaching the Moon.

items.truth: The Moon’s orbital tilt helps explain why eclipses do not occur every month.
items.lie: A solar and lunar eclipse must both occur every month.
items.explanation: The tilted orbit usually carries the Moon above or below the required alignment.

items.truth: We generally see the same side of the Moon because its rotation and orbital periods are matched.
items.lie: We see the same side of the Moon because the Moon never rotates.
items.explanation: Synchronous rotation turns the Moon once during each orbit.

items.truth: The far side of the Moon receives sunlight.
items.lie: The far side of the Moon is permanently dark.
items.explanation: Both sides experience sunlight and darkness; far side does not mean dark side.

items.truth: Gravity keeps planets in orbit around the Sun.
items.lie: Planets remain in orbit because no force acts on them.
items.explanation: Gravity continuously changes the direction of their motion.

items.truth: Astronauts in low Earth orbit still experience Earth’s gravity.
items.lie: Astronauts float in low Earth orbit because Earth’s gravity has ended there.
items.explanation: They and their spacecraft are in continuous free fall, producing apparent weightlessness.

items.truth: The Solar System is part of the Milky Way galaxy.
items.lie: The Milky Way galaxy is a small part of the Solar System.
items.explanation: The galaxy contains vast numbers of stars, including the Sun and its planets.

items.truth: Stars are much farther away than the planets in our Solar System.
items.lie: All visible stars lie between Earth and the outer planets.
items.explanation: Other stars lie far beyond the Solar System.

items.truth: A meteor is the visible phenomenon produced when space material enters the atmosphere.
items.lie: A meteor is a star physically falling out of the sky.
items.explanation: A meteoroid entering the atmosphere produces the light; it is not a falling star.

items.truth: A meteorite is space material that reaches the ground.
items.lie: A meteorite is any bright streak that never reaches the ground.
items.explanation: Material surviving atmospheric passage and reaching the surface is a meteorite.

items.truth: Earth’s crust is divided into tectonic plates that move.
items.lie: Earth’s tectonic plates are permanently fixed in place.
items.explanation: Plate motion occurs slowly over geological time.

items.truth: At a divergent boundary, tectonic plates move apart.
items.lie: At a divergent boundary, tectonic plates move towards each other.
items.explanation: Divergence means separation; convergence means approach.

items.truth: At a transform boundary, plates slide past one another.
items.lie: At a transform boundary, one plate must always sink beneath the other.
items.explanation: Transform motion is mainly sideways; subduction occurs at some convergent boundaries.

items.truth: Earthquakes can occur when rocks suddenly slip along a fault.
items.lie: Earthquakes are caused only by volcanic eruptions.
items.explanation: Fault slip can release stored elastic energy independently of volcanic activity.

items.truth: Weathering breaks down rock in place.
items.lie: Weathering is the transport of all broken rock to a new location.
items.explanation: Weathering breaks material down; erosion involves removal and transport.

items.truth: Erosion can move sediment by water, wind or ice.
items.lie: Erosion can be caused only by liquid water.
items.explanation: Several agents transport sediment, including wind and moving ice.

items.truth: Metamorphic rock forms when existing rock changes under heat and pressure without fully melting.
items.lie: Metamorphic rock forms only after existing rock completely melts.
items.explanation: Full melting followed by solidification forms igneous rock; metamorphism occurs largely in the solid state.

items.truth: Sedimentary rocks can contain fossils.
items.lie: Fossils form only inside molten lava.
items.explanation: Burial and preservation in sediments can retain evidence of past organisms.

items.truth: The water cycle includes evaporation, condensation and precipitation.
items.lie: Water moves through the water cycle only as a liquid.
items.explanation: Water changes state and moves among atmosphere, land and water bodies.

items.truth: Groundwater occupies pores and cracks in rock and sediment.
items.lie: All groundwater forms large open underground rivers.
items.explanation: Most groundwater is held in small spaces rather than open channels.

items.truth: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes longer-term patterns.
items.lie: Weather and climate both mean only today’s temperature.
items.explanation: Climate summarises patterns and variability over extended periods.

items.truth: Greenhouse gases absorb and emit some outgoing infrared radiation.
items.lie: Greenhouse gases warm Earth only by reflecting all sunlight back to the surface.
items.explanation: Their interaction with infrared radiation affects Earth’s energy balance; this differs from simply reflecting sunlight.

items.truth: Earth’s tilt is the main cause of its seasons.
items.lie: Earth’s changing distance from the Sun is the main cause of its seasons.
items.explanation: Axial tilt changes day length and the angle of sunlight. The hemispheres experience opposite seasons at the same time.

items.truth: The Moon’s ordinary phases result from our changing view of its sunlit half.
items.lie: The Moon’s ordinary phases are caused by Earth’s shadow covering it each month.
items.explanation: As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different portions of its illuminated half. Earth’s shadow causes a lunar eclipse, not the usual phases.

items.truth: The Sun is a star.
items.lie: The Sun is a planet.
items.explanation: The Sun produces energy through nuclear fusion in its core. Planets orbit stars and do not sustain the same kind of core fusion.

items.truth: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and solidifies.
items.lie: Igneous rock forms only by compacting layers of sediment.
items.explanation: Cooling magma or lava forms igneous rock. Compaction and cementation are processes associated with many sedimentary rocks.

items.truth: Repeated measurements can help estimate random variation.
items.lie: Repeated measurements always remove systematic error.
items.explanation: Repeats reveal spread and can improve estimates, but a consistent bias can remain in every measurement.

items.truth: A correlation alone does not establish that one variable causes another.
items.lie: A correlation proves that one variable causes another.
items.explanation: An association may have alternative explanations, including confounding variables. Causal claims need additional evidence.

items.truth: A scientific theory is an explanatory framework supported by evidence.
items.lie: A scientific theory is simply an unsupported guess.
items.explanation: Scientific theories explain evidence and generate testable predictions. The scientific meaning differs from casual use of “theory”.

items.truth: An observation can involve a measuring instrument.
items.lie: An observation must be made using unaided human senses only.
items.explanation: Instruments extend our senses and provide quantitative measurements.

items.truth: An inference is an interpretation drawn from observations and reasoning.
items.lie: An inference is identical to the raw observation itself.
items.explanation: An observation describes evidence; an inference explains or interprets it.

items.truth: A prediction describes an expected outcome.
items.lie: A prediction is always a measurement already collected.
items.explanation: Predictions concern what is expected under specified conditions.

items.truth: A useful scientific hypothesis should be testable against evidence.
items.lie: A scientific hypothesis is useful only if no observation could ever challenge it.
items.explanation: Testability allows evidence to support or challenge a proposed explanation.

items.truth: A fair test usually changes one independent variable while controlling relevant alternatives.
items.lie: A fair test requires changing every variable at the same time.
items.explanation: Controlling other influences helps isolate the effect being investigated.

items.truth: The independent variable is the factor deliberately changed in a controlled experiment.
items.lie: The independent variable is always the measurement taken as the result.
items.explanation: The dependent variable is measured in response to the independent variable.

items.truth: The dependent variable is the response measured in an experiment.
items.lie: The dependent variable must always be kept constant.
items.explanation: It is measured to determine how it responds to the changed factor.

items.truth: A controlled variable is kept consistent to reduce unwanted influences.
items.lie: A controlled variable is deliberately changed to produce the main result.
items.explanation: Consistent conditions help isolate the independent variable’s effect.

items.truth: A control group can provide a baseline for comparison.
items.lie: A control group must receive a larger dose of the treatment than every experimental group.
items.explanation: A baseline helps assess effects of the treatment; its design depends on the investigation.

items.truth: A larger sample can improve an estimate without removing sampling bias.
items.lie: Increasing sample size automatically removes every form of bias.
items.explanation: A large unrepresentative sample can still systematically misrepresent the population.

items.truth: Accuracy concerns agreement with an accepted or reference value.
items.lie: Accuracy means only that repeated measurements are close to one another.
items.explanation: Closeness among repeat readings is precision, which does not guarantee accuracy.

items.truth: Precise measurements can all be inaccurate.
items.lie: Precise measurements must always be accurate.
items.explanation: A systematic offset can make readings tightly grouped but far from the reference value.

items.truth: Random error contributes to scatter among repeated readings.
items.lie: Random error always shifts every reading by exactly the same amount.
items.explanation: A fixed shift is systematic; random variation changes unpredictably among measurements.

items.truth: A zero error in a measuring instrument can create systematic error.
items.lie: A zero error is guaranteed to disappear simply by taking more repeats.
items.explanation: An offset can remain in all readings unless it is identified and corrected.

items.truth: Recording units is essential when reporting measured quantities.
items.lie: A measured number has the same meaning regardless of its unit.
items.explanation: Five metres and five centimetres represent different lengths.

items.truth: Graph axes should identify the quantities and their units.
items.lie: Graph axes need numbers only; labels and units are unnecessary.
items.explanation: Labels and units make the plotted measurements interpretable.

items.truth: The independent variable is usually placed on the horizontal axis.
items.lie: The independent variable is always placed on the vertical axis.
items.explanation: The usual convention places the independent variable on x and the dependent variable on y.

items.truth: A best-fit line summarises a trend rather than necessarily passing through every point.
items.lie: A best-fit line must join every point in the order it was measured.
items.explanation: A fitted trend reflects the overall relationship rather than every fluctuation.

items.truth: An outlier should be investigated before deciding whether to exclude it.
items.lie: An outlier should always be deleted because it makes a graph untidy.
items.explanation: An unusual value may reflect a mistake or real variation; exclusions need reasons.

items.truth: Extrapolation estimates beyond the measured data range.
items.lie: Extrapolation estimates only between measured data points.
items.explanation: Interpolation is within the data range; extrapolation extends beyond it.

items.truth: Extrapolations can be less reliable when the relationship changes outside the measured range.
items.lie: A straight trend over a small range proves the same trend continues forever.
items.explanation: Relationships may change under conditions not represented by the observations.

items.truth: A model represents selected features of a system.
items.lie: A scientific model must reproduce every feature of the real system exactly.
items.explanation: Models simplify reality for a purpose and have limitations.

items.truth: Evidence can lead scientists to revise a model.
items.lie: A scientific model can never change once it appears in a textbook.
items.explanation: Scientific models are assessed and refined as evidence develops.

items.truth: Peer review can identify weaknesses but does not guarantee a study is correct.
items.lie: Peer review guarantees that every conclusion in a study is permanently correct.
items.explanation: Review is a quality check, not an infallible guarantee.

items.truth: A method should provide enough detail for others to attempt the investigation.
items.lie: A method should omit measurement steps so others must guess them.
items.explanation: Clear procedures support reproducibility and meaningful comparison.

items.truth: A conclusion should be supported by the collected evidence.
items.lie: A conclusion should be chosen before the experiment and kept regardless of the results.
items.explanation: Evidence should guide conclusions, including when results challenge expectations.

items.truth: An experiment that does not support a hypothesis can still provide useful evidence.
items.lie: An experiment is scientifically worthless if it does not support the hypothesis.
items.explanation: Unexpected results can test assumptions, constrain explanations and guide further work.
